questions.stem:
A 2 kg mass is being pulled up a slope by a string of tension 10 Newtons. The slope is at an angle \(\theta\) to the horizontal and the coefficient of friction is 0.3. As well as friction, the forces of gravity \(g\) and the normal are also acting.

Copy the diagram.

By resolving forces with components along and perpendicular to the slope, find the net force \(F_{net}\) in Newtons up the slope.

steps.explain: Draw all the forces on the mass: tension \(T=10\) up the slope, friction \(F\) down the slope (it opposes the motion), weight \(mg=2g\) straight down, and the normal \(N\) perpendicular to the slope.

steps.explain: Resolve the weight into components: \(mg\sin\theta\) down the slope and \(mg\cos\theta\) into the slope.
Perpendicular to the slope there is no motion, so the forces balance.
Common slips: swapping \(\sin\) and \(\cos\) in the components, or using \(N=mg\) instead of \(mg\cos\theta\).

keyPoints.text: resolving forces with components along and perpendicular to the slope
keyPoints.note: Perpendicular: N = mg cos θ. Along: F_net = T − μN − mg sin θ.

questions.stem:
An object of mass \(m\) rests on a plane inclined at a variable angle \(\theta\) from the horizontal. It experiences a friction force, \(F\), and a normal force, \(N\). The friction force is \(F=\mu N\) where \(\mu\) is constant. The normal force, \(N\), is equal in magnitude to the force the object exerts on the plane perpendicular to the plane. Let \(\alpha\) be the maximal angle that the plane can be tilted before the object begins to slide down the plane.

For some \(\theta\gt\alpha\), a horizontal force \(H\) is applied to the object so that if \(H\) is sufficiently large, then the object will slide up the plane and if \(H\) is sufficiently small, then the object will slide down the plane.

Show that, for the object to remain motionless, \(H\) must satisfy \(mg\tan(\theta-\alpha)\le H\le mg\tan(\theta+\alpha)\)

questions.hint: μ = tan α from the limiting case; then N = H sin θ + mg cos θ, and write the 'no slide up' and 'no slide down' inequalities.

steps.explain: First find \(\mu\). At the maximal angle \(\alpha\) (no \(H\)), friction is at its limit and balances the slope component of gravity.
Now apply \(H\) horizontally at angle \(\theta\). Resolve perpendicular to the plane: both \(H\) and gravity push into the plane.

steps.explain: No sliding up: the up-slope push \(H\cos\theta\) must not beat gravity plus maximum friction (friction acts down-slope).
No sliding down: gravity's slope component must not beat \(H\cos\theta\) plus maximum friction (now acting up-slope).

questions.answer: At angle α (limiting): F = mg sin α, N = mg cos α ⇒ μ = tan α. With H at angle θ: N = H sin θ + mg cos θ. No sliding up: H cos θ ≤ mg sin θ + μN = mg sin θ + tan α(H sin θ + mg cos θ); dividing by cos θ: H(1 − tan θ tan α) ≤ mg(tan θ + tan α) ⇒ H ≤ mg tan(θ + α). No sliding down: mg sin θ ≤ H cos θ + tan α(H sin θ + mg cos θ) ⇒ mg(tan θ − tan α) ≤ H(1 + tan θ tan α) ⇒ H ≥ mg tan(θ − α).

keyPoints.text: Show that, for the object to remain motionless
keyPoints.note: First get μ = tan α. Then friction can act either way: write one inequality for each direction.

questions.stem:
A body of mass 1 kg is moving in a horizontal straight line and is acted on by a force \(F=8x^3+36x\) newtons, where \(x\) is the displacement of the body in metres, measured from the origin.
If the body is initially one metre to the right of the origin with velocity of 11 m/s, find the displacement function \(x(t)\).
questions.hint: v² turns out to be a perfect square, (2x² + 9)²; then integrate dt/dx = 1/(2x² + 9).

steps.explain: Mass 1 kg, so \(\ddot x=8x^3+36x\). Use \(\ddot x=\frac{d}{dx}(\frac12v^2)\).
Take the positive root, since \(v=11\gt 0\) at \(x=1\) (and \(2x^2+9\) is never 0).

keyPoints.note: Use ẍ = d/dx(½v²); v² = (2x² + 9)². Then separate dx/dt = 2x² + 9.

questions.stem: Assume that the tides rise and fall in simple harmonic motion. At low tide the depth of water in a harbour was 6 m deep, and at high tide it was 10 m deep. Low tide was at 8:00 am and the high tide following it was at 3:00 pm.

parts.stem: What is the amplitude of the motion?

steps.explain: The amplitude is half the distance between the lowest and highest positions.
4 m is the full range (high minus low), not the amplitude.

keyPoints.note: Amplitude is half the range between low and high tide.

parts.stem: What is the period of the motion?
parts.hint: Low to high is half a period.

steps.explain: From low tide (8:00 am) to the next high tide (3:00 pm) is 7 hours — that is half a cycle.

keyPoints.note: Low tide to the next high tide is only half a cycle.

parts.stem: What was the depth of the harbour at 11:30 am?
parts.hint: 11:30 am is halfway between low and high tide.

steps.explain: 11:30 am is 3.5 hours after low tide — exactly halfway between low (8:00) and high (3:00).
Halfway in time between an extreme and the next extreme, an SHM particle is at the centre of motion.

keyPoints.note: Halfway in time between low and high tide is the centre of the motion.

parts.stem: Starting with \(y=a\cos(nt+\alpha)+c\) and by using your answers from parts (i), (ii) and (iii), show that the depth \(y\) m of the water in the harbour is given by \(y=8-2\cos\left(\frac{\pi}{7}t\right)\) where \(t\) is the number of hours after 8:00 am.
parts.hint: a = 2, c = 8, n = 2π/14; find α from y = 6 at t = 0.

steps.explain: At \(t=0\) (8:00 am) it is low tide, \(y=6\).

parts.answer: a = 2 (amplitude), c = 8 (centre), and \(\frac{2\pi}{n}=14\Rightarrow n=\frac{\pi}{7}\). So \(y=2\cos\left(\frac{\pi}{7}t+\alpha\right)+8\). At t = 0 (low tide) y = 6: \(6=2\cos\alpha+8\Rightarrow\cos\alpha=-1\Rightarrow\alpha=\pi\). Then \(y=2\cos\left(\frac{\pi}{7}t+\pi\right)+8=8-2\cos\left(\frac{\pi}{7}t\right)\).

keyPoints.note: Use a = 2, centre c = 8, n = 2π/period, and low tide (y = 6) at t = 0 to find α.

parts.stem: A boat needs at least 9 m of water to pass through the harbour. Between which times after 8:00 am on this day could the ship navigate safely through the harbour?
parts.hint: Solve 8 − 2cos(πt/7) = 9, then convert hours to clock times.

steps.explain: Within the first cycle \(0\le\frac{\pi}{7}t\le2\pi\), \(\cos=-\frac12\) at \(\frac{2\pi}{3}\) and \(\frac{4\pi}{3}\).
Convert to clock times: \(\frac{14}{3}\) h = 4 h 40 min, \(\frac{28}{3}\) h = 9 h 20 min after 8:00 am.
The depth is at least 9 m between these times (the top of the curve).

keyPoints.note: Solve cos(πt/7) = −1/2 in the first cycle, then add the times to 8:00 am.

questions.stem: The velocity of a particle at \(x=-3\) with simple harmonic motion described by \(\ddot{x}=-12(x+3)\) where the amplitude is 4, is:
questions.hint: Find the centre and n² from ẍ = −n²(x − c), then use v² = n²(a² − (x − c)²).

steps.explain: Compare with \(\ddot x=-n^2(x-c)\): the centre of motion is \(c=-3\) and \(n^2=12\).
At \(x=-3\) the particle is at the centre (where speed is greatest), and the amplitude is \(a=4\).
Both signs are possible because the particle passes through the centre in both directions. (0 would be the velocity at an end point \(x=-3\pm4\).)

keyPoints.note: Centre x = −3 and n² = 12. At the centre v² = n²a².

questions.stem: The acceleration of a particle \(P\) moving along the \(x\)-axis is given by \(\ddot{x}=4x^3-12x\).

parts.stem: If \(P\) is initially at the origin with velocity \(u\), show that its velocity is given by \(v^2=2x^4-12x^2+u^2\).

keyPoints.text: show that its velocity is given by
keyPoints.note: Write ẍ as d/dx(½v²), integrate, then use v = u at x = 0.

parts.stem: If \(u=4\), show that the particle oscillates within the interval \(-\sqrt2\le x\le\sqrt2\).

steps.explain: Since \(v^2\ge0\), the particle can only be where the right side is non-negative: \(|x|\le\sqrt2\) or \(|x|\ge2\). It starts at \(x=0\), and between \(\sqrt2\) and 2 we would have \(v^2\lt 0\), so it can never get past \(\pm\sqrt2\).
At \(x=\pm\sqrt2\) the particle stops (\(v=0\)). Check the acceleration there.
The acceleration points back towards the origin at each end, so the particle turns around. Hence it oscillates in \(-\sqrt2\le x\le\sqrt2\).

parts.answer: With u = 4: \(v^2=2x^4-12x^2+16=2(x^2-4)(x^2-2)\). \(v^2\ge0\) for \(|x|\le\sqrt2\) or \(|x|\ge2\). Starting at x = 0 the particle is in \(-\sqrt2\le x\le\sqrt2\) and cannot pass beyond ±√2 (v² < 0 for √2 < |x| < 2). At x = ±√2, v = 0 and \(\ddot x=4x(x^2-3)=\mp4\sqrt2\neq0\), pointing back towards the origin, so it turns around and oscillates in \(-\sqrt2\le x\le\sqrt2\).

keyPoints.note: v² ≥ 0 restricts x; check v = 0 and the direction of ẍ at ±√2.

parts.stem:
Is the motion referred to in part (ii) simple harmonic motion?
Give a reason for your answer.

steps.explain: SHM requires the acceleration to be a negative constant times the displacement from a fixed centre.
Here the acceleration is cubic in \(x\).
It is not linear in \(x\), so the motion is not SHM — even though the particle does oscillate. Oscillating is not enough on its own.

options: Yes: \(\ddot x\) is zero at the centre \(x=0\).
No: the particle never comes to rest.
No: \(\ddot x=4x\left(x^2-3\right)\) is not of the form \(-n^2(x-c)\).
Yes: the particle oscillates between two points.

questions.stem: When an aircraft touches down on a runway, two different retarding forces combine to ultimately bring the aircraft to rest. parts.answer: For 0 ≤ t ≤ 10 only friction acts: \(M\ddot x=-\frac15M\Rightarrow\ddot x=-0.2\). So \(v=80-0.2t\) and \(x=80t-0.1t^2\) (v = 80, x = 0 at t = 0). At t = 10: v = 80 − 2 = 78 m/s and x = 800 − 10 = 790 m.

questions.stem:
The Covid-19 1.5 metre rule is based on the premise that a person emits droplets from a height 1.8 m above ground at an angle \(\theta\) from the horizontal so that the maximum range on the ground is 1.5 metres. Show that the maximum speed \(V\) m/s of the droplets launched is given by

\(V=\sqrt{\frac{15g}{22}}\).  (Assume there is no air resistance.)

[Hint: you can assume which angle gives the maximum range…..]
questions.hint: Use θ = 45°, write x(t) and y(t) from height 1.8, then put x = 1.5, y = 0.

steps.explain: Set up axes with the origin on the ground directly below the mouth. Using the hint, take the angle for maximum range, \(\theta=45^\circ\).
Integrate with the initial conditions \(\dot x=V\cos\theta\), \(\dot y=V\sin\theta\), \(x=0\), \(y=1.8\) at \(t=0\).
The droplet lands at \(x=1.5\), \(y=0\). Find the time from \(x\).

questions.answer: Take θ = 45° (maximum range). With the origin on the ground below the mouth: \(x=Vt\cos\theta=\frac{Vt}{\sqrt2}\), \(y=1.8+Vt\sin\theta-\frac{gt^2}{2}=1.8+\frac{Vt}{\sqrt2}-\frac{gt^2}{2}\). The droplet lands at x = 1.5, y = 0: \(t=\frac{1.5\sqrt2}{V}\), so \(0=1.8+1.5-\frac{g}{2}\cdot\frac{4.5}{V^2}\), i.e. \(3.3=\frac{2.25g}{V^2}\), \(V^2=\frac{2.25g}{3.3}=\frac{15g}{22}\), so \(V=\sqrt{\frac{15g}{22}}\).

keyPoints.text: from a height 1.8 m above ground
keyPoints.note: Start y at 1.8 (not 0). Use θ = 45° and the landing point x = 1.5, y = 0.
